abstract: |
  Birds are widely expected to shrink as the climate warms, but few tropical studies span decades. In the central Amazon, mean body mass fell in all 77 species studied and a third of species lengthened their wings. We analysed 24 years (1995–2018) of morphology from 73 passerine species (12,571 live-capture records; ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS) across the Brazilian Atlantic Forest, a region that warmed by about 0.25°C per decade. The records came from 47 research programmes whose sites changed over time, so we modelled contributor and municipality explicitly and checked by simulation that these models recover trends planted in the real sampling structure. Unadjusted models suggested a steep wing-length decline and increases in bill width and trait variability. Once sampling turnover was modelled, the wing decline was less than half as steep (−1.0% per decade, 95% credible interval spanning zero), and the bill-width and variability changes disappeared. Body mass declined by 0.9% per decade, close to the mean Amazonian rate of 1.0%, but its interval spanned zero (−2.8 to +1.0%). Responses varied strongly among species, and most species showed no change distinguishable from zero. Wings did not lengthen, and among individuals measured for both traits, mass tended to be retained relative to wing length. Neither trait was associated with interannual temperature anomalies. Atlantic Forest passerines thus show neither the consistent mass loss across species nor the wing elongation reported from the Amazon, although their average mass change is compatible with the Amazonian rate. Compiled trait databases can extend long-term monitoring to under-studied tropical regions, but only when sampling structure is modelled: ignoring it here would have more than doubled the estimated wing decline.
summary-statement: |
  Atlantic Forest birds lost mass at about the Amazonian average rate but without its consistency across species, and modelling sampling turnover more than halved the apparent wing decline.
plain-language-summary: |
  As global temperatures rise, many animals are expected to become smaller or change shape to cope with heat. In the intact Amazon rainforest, every bird species studied became lighter over four decades, and many grew longer wings. We asked whether birds in another tropical forest, the Brazilian Atlantic Forest, changed in the same way, using 24 years of field measurements (1995–2018) of 73 perching-bird species. On average, Atlantic Forest birds became lighter at about the same rate as Amazonian birds, but the estimate was uncertain and species went in both directions rather than all declining together. Wings did not grow longer, and bills did not change. The data came from many research groups whose field sites changed over the years, and simpler analyses exaggerated how much the birds had changed: allowing for who collected the data, and where, more than halved the apparent shortening of wings. Computer simulations confirmed that this correction recovers real trends rather than hiding them.

# format a count with a thousands separator for inline use
.n <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
# format a signed estimate / CI bound to 2 dp with a true minus sign
.s <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", x))
# format a signed value to 1 dp with a true minus sign
.s1 <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", x))
# format a signed estimate to 4 dp with a true minus sign
.s4 <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.4f", x))
# format a p-value for inline use
.rp <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else paste("=", sprintf("%.3f", p))

# pull row from cw_phylo$before_after with optional term filtering
.cw <- function(mod, term = NULL) {
  r <- cw_phylo$before_after[cw_phylo$before_after$model == mod, ]
  if (!is.null(term)) r <- r[r$term == term, ]
  if (nrow(r) == 0) return(list(b = "NA", lo = "NA", hi = "NA", dec = "NA", dec_lo = "NA", dec_hi = "NA", n = "NA"))
  list(
    b      = .s(r$estimate[1]),
    lo     = .s(r$ci_lo[1]),
    hi     = .s(r$ci_hi[1]),
    dec    = .s1(r$mm_per_decade[1]),
    dec_lo = .s1(r$mm_per_decade_lo[1]),
    dec_hi = .s1(r$mm_per_decade_hi[1]),
    n      = .n(r$N[1])
  )
}

# multi-trait comparisons from multi_phylo
.mt_phylo <- function(trait_name, mod, term = "scaled_yr") {
  df <- multi_phylo$comparison_lme4
  r <- df[df$trait == trait_name & df$model == mod & df$term == term, ]
  if (nrow(r) == 0) return(list(b = "NA", b2 = "NA", lo = "NA", hi = "NA", lo2 = "NA", hi2 = "NA", pct = "NA", pct_lo = "NA", pct_hi = "NA", n = "NA"))
  list(
    b      = .s4(r$phylo_estimate[1]),
    b2     = .s(r$phylo_estimate[1]),
    lo     = .s4(r$phylo_lower[1]),
    hi     = .s4(r$phylo_upper[1]),
    lo2    = .s(r$phylo_lower[1]),
    hi2    = .s(r$phylo_upper[1]),
    pct    = .s1(r$phylo_pct_per_decade[1]),
    pct_lo = .s1(r$phylo_pct_lower[1]),
    pct_hi = .s1(r$phylo_pct_upper[1]),
    n      = .n(r$phylo_n[1])
  )
}

multi_lme4 <- readRDS("../Analysis/output/multitrait_results.rds")
.mt_lme4 <- function(trait_name, mod, term = "scaled_yr") {
  df <- multi_lme4$table
  r <- df[df$trait == trait_name & df$model == mod & df$term == term, ]
  if (nrow(r) == 0) return(list(b = "NA", b2 = "NA", lo = "NA", hi = "NA", lo2 = "NA", hi2 = "NA", pct = "NA", pct_lo = "NA", pct_hi = "NA", n = "NA"))
  list(
    b      = .s4(r$estimate[1]),
    b2     = .s(r$estimate[1]),
    lo     = .s4(r$lower[1]),
    hi     = .s4(r$upper[1]),
    lo2    = .s(r$lower[1]),
    hi2    = .s(r$upper[1]),
    pct    = .s1(r$pct_per_decade[1]),
    pct_lo = .s1(r$pct_per_decade_lower[1]),
    pct_hi = .s1(r$pct_per_decade_upper[1]),
    n      = .n(r$n[1])
  )
}

clim_tm <- clim$pooled[clim$pooled$variable == "tmean" & clim$pooled$weighting == "unweighted + year RE", ]
.clim_row <- function(v, dp) { r <- clim$pooled[clim$pooled$variable == v & clim$pooled$weighting == "unweighted + year RE", ]
  f <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf(paste0("%+.", dp, "f"), x))
  list(b = f(r$slope_per_decade), lo = f(r$lower), hi = f(r$upper), est = r$slope_per_decade) }
clim_t <- .clim_row("tmean", 3); clim_p <- .clim_row("prec_annual", 1); clim_s <- .clim_row("spei12_dec", 3)
clim_t_dec2 <- sprintf("%.2f", clim_t$est)                    # rounded rate for the Discussion
clim_t_tot  <- sprintf("%+.2f", clim_t$est * (2018 - 1995) / 10) # linear warming over 1995-2018

# ---- Bayesian (Stan) tier: the source of every model estimate in the text ----
# bayes_summary.rds from bayes_aggregate.R (posterior pooled over 20 trees);
# bayes_derived.rds from bayes_derived.R (species slopes, diet percentiles).
bayes <- readRDS("../Analysis/output/bayes/bayes_summary.rds")
bder  <- readRDS("../Analysis/output/bayes/bayes_derived.rds")
DEC   <- bder$dec                      # SD-of-year units per decade
.p2   <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
# posterior probability with its relation sign: "= 0.83", or "> 0.99" / "< 0.01"
# when it rounds to 1 or 0 (a posterior probability is never exactly 1)
.pp   <- function(x) if (x >= 0.995) "> 0.99" else if (x < 0.005) "< 0.01" else paste("=", .p2(x))
# signed formatters with a true minus sign and an explicit plus
.ss1 <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%+.1f", x)); .ss <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%+.2f", x))
.ss4 <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%+.4f", x))
# one coefficient of one fit; scale = "mm" (per-decade on the response scale),
# "pct" (log response: % per decade), "sigma" (log residual SD: % per decade),
# "raw" (per unit of the covariate, e.g. per degree C of anomaly)
.bz <- function(fit, par, scale = c("mm", "mm2", "pct", "sigma", "raw")) {
  scale <- match.arg(scale)
  r <- bayes$fixed[bayes$fixed$fit == fit & bayes$fixed$par == par, ]
  na <- list(b = "NA", lo = "NA", hi = "NA", P = "NA", Ppos = "NA", n = "NA")
  if (nrow(r) != 1) return(na)
  f <- switch(scale, mm = function(x) .ss1(x * DEC), mm2 = function(x) .ss(x * DEC), pct = function(x) .ss1(100 * (exp(x * DEC) - 1)),
              sigma = function(x) .ss1(100 * (exp(x * DEC) - 1)), raw = function(x) .ss4(x))
  n <- bayes$meta$n[bayes$meta$fit == fit]
  list(b = f(r$estimate), lo = f(r$lower), hi = f(r$upper), P = .pp(r$p_neg), Ppos = .pp(1 - r$p_neg),
       n = .n(n), est = r$estimate)
}
# sampler diagnostics and agreement with REML, over the fits quoted in the text
local({
  d <- bayes$diag; cm <- bayes$comparison[!grepl("__pcor$", bayes$comparison$fit) &
    grepl("scaled_yr|dT|yr_within|yr_src|yr_mean|:", bayes$comparison$par), ]
  dg <- bder$diag_focal; ds <- bder$diag_sd_spp_int
  bz <<- list(n_fits = nrow(bayes$meta), n_trees = max(bayes$fixed$n_trees),
              foc_rhat = sprintf("%.3f", dg[["rhat_max"]]), foc_ess = .n(round(dg[["ess_bulk_pooled_min"]])),
              foc_ess_tail = .n(round(dg[["ess_tail_pooled_min"]])),
              sd_rhat = sprintf("%.3f", ds[["rhat_max"]]), sd_ess = .n(round(ds[["ess_bulk_min"]])),
              rhat_max = sprintf("%.3f", max(d$rhat_max)),
              ess_min = .n(round(min(d$ess_bulk_min))),
              shift_max = sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(cm$diff_in_sd))),
              sd_ratio_max = sprintf("%.2f", max(cm$sd_ratio)))
})
.fid <- c(
  w0 = "atlantic_parallel_controlled__001__conc.wing.length__M0",

  w3cc = "atlantic_parallel_controlled__023__conc.wing.length__M3_cc",

  bl0 = "atlantic_multitrait__005__y", bl1 = "atlantic_multitrait__006__y",
  bl3 = "atlantic_multitrait__007__y", blw = "atlantic_multitrait__008__y",
  s1 = "atlantic_variance_sigma__002__conc.wing.length__S1", s3 = "atlantic_variance_sigma__004__conc.wing.length__S3",
  s7 = "atlantic_variance_sigma__009__conc.wing.length__S7",
  dA0 = "atlantic_diet_interaction__002__conc.wing.length", dA1 = "atlantic_diet_interaction__006__conc.wing.length",
  dB1 = "atlantic_diet_interaction__012__conc.wing.length",
  th_w = "referee_reruns__001__wing__site", th_m = "referee_reruns__003__lnmass__site",
  th_i = "referee_reruns__005__iso__site", th_iy = "referee_reruns__006__iso__site",
  th_id = "referee_reruns__013__iso__site", th_il = "referee_reruns__014__iso__site",
  # year-only isometry models on all shared records (no anomaly required;

  iso_p = "referee_reruns__015__iso__all", iso_f = "referee_reruns__016__iso__all",

    list(b = .ss1(100 * (exp(r$estimate) - 1)), lo = .ss1(100 * (exp(r$lower) - 1)),
         hi = .ss1(100 * (exp(r$upper) - 1)), P = .pp(r$p_neg)) })
# diet: year x invertebrate share (mm per SD year per SD diet), category contrast, percentile slopes
.bzraw2 <- function(fit, par) { x <- .bz(fit, par, "raw"); if (x$b == "NA") return(x)
  r <- bayes$fixed[bayes$fixed$fit == fit & bayes$fixed$par == par, ]
  modifyList(x, list(b = .ss(r$estimate), lo = .ss(r$lower), hi = .ss(r$upper))) }
b_dA0 <- .bzraw2(.fid[["dA0"]], "b_scaled_yr:diet_inv_std"); b_dA1 <- .bzraw2(.fid[["dA1"]], "b_scaled_yr:diet_inv_std")

.dq <- function(k) { q <- bder$diet_quantile_slopes; r <- q[q$quantile == k, ]
  list(b = .ss(r$estimate), lo = .ss(r$lower), hi = .ss(r$upper), P = .pp(r$p_neg), inv = r$diet_inv) }
b_p10 <- .dq("p10"); b_p90 <- .dq("p90")
# thermal anomaly (per degree C) and isometry (% per decade)

n_iso_spp <- sum(bayes$species_slope_dev$fit == .fid[["iso_f"]])
# species posterior means (fixed + deviation) of the shared-record wing and mass
# slopes: how many fall in the longer-wing / lower-mass quadrant (Fig. isometry B)
n_iso_decoupled <- local({
  sp <- function(fit) { b0 <- bayes$fixed$estimate[bayes$fixed$fit == fit & bayes$fixed$par == "b_scaled_yr"]
    d <- bayes$species_slope_dev[bayes$species_slope_dev$fit == fit, ]; setNames(b0 + d$estimate, d$par) }
  w <- sp(.fid[["lnw"]]); m <- sp(.fid[["lnm"]])[names(w)]
  if (!length(w)) NA else sum(w > 0 & m < 0, na.rm = TRUE) })
# random-effect SDs (mm) of the fully adjusted wing model, posterior means
.vc <- function(par) .s(bayes$varcomp$estimate[bayes$varcomp$fit == .fid[["w3"]] & bayes$varcomp$par == par])
cw_sd_src <- .vc("sd_src"); cw_sd_site <- .vc("sd_site")

# posterior summary of a variance-component parameter, e.g. h2_slope
.vcz <- function(fit, par) { r <- bayes$varcomp[bayes$varcomp$fit == fit & bayes$varcomp$par == par, ]
  if (nrow(r) != 1) return(list(b = "NA", lo = "NA", hi = "NA"))
  m2 <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", x))
  list(b = m2(r$estimate), lo = m2(r$lower), hi = m2(r$upper)) }
h2s_w <- .vcz(.fid[["w3pcor"]], "h2_slope"); h2s_i <- .vcz(.fid[["iso_fpcor"]], "h2_slope")
cor_w <- .vcz(.fid[["w3pcor"]], "cor_phylo_int_slope")
# REML likelihood-ratio test for a phylogenetic slope component (atlantic_phylo_slopes.R, wing fully adjusted)
.lrt <- readRDS("../Analysis/output/phylo_slopes/phylo_slopes_results.rds")$wing_M3$lrt
lrt_w <- list(sig = sum(.lrt$p_boundary < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), n = sum(is.finite(.lrt$p_boundary)),
              p_med = sprintf("%.2f", median(.lrt$p_boundary, na.rm = TRUE)))
# lagged anomalies, REML across 50 trees (referee_anomaly_lag.R)
lag <- readRDS("../Analysis/output/referee_reruns/anomaly_lag.rds")
.lg <- function(tbl, response, term, dp = 4) { r <- lag[[tbl]]; r <- r[r$response == response & r$term == term, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1); fm <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf(paste0("%+.", dp, "f"), x))
  list(b = fm(r$estimate), lo = fm(r$lower), hi = fm(r$upper), p = .rp(r$p)) }
lg1_i <- .lg("L1", "isometry contrast lnM-3lnL", "dT_lag1"); lg12_i <- .lg("L12", "isometry contrast lnM-3lnL", "dT_lag12")
lg1_w <- .lg("L1", "wing length (mm)", "dT_lag1", 2); lg12_w <- .lg("L12", "wing length (mm)", "dT_lag12", 2)
lg1_m <- .lg("L1", "log body mass", "dT_lag1"); lg12_m <- .lg("L12", "log body mass", "dT_lag12")

rr          <- readRDS("../Analysis/output/referee_reruns/referee_reruns.rds")

# accessors for the referee re-run tables (Analysis/scripts/referee_reruns.R).
# Every number quoted from these blocks is pulled from the saved object, never
# typed into the text.
.rr_row <- function(tbl, ...) {
  f <- list(...); keep <- rep(TRUE, nrow(tbl))
  for (nm in names(f)) keep <- keep & tbl[[nm]] == f[[nm]]
  r <- tbl[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1L)
  r
}
# thermal-anomaly effects (E1-E3)
rr_therm <- function(model, response, term = "dT", tbl = NULL) {
  tb <- if (is.null(tbl)) rr$E3 else tbl
  r <- .rr_row(tb, model = model, response = response, term = term)
  list(z = .s(r$z), p = .rp(r$p), b = .s4(r$estimate), se = sprintf("%.4f", r$se),
       lo = .s4(r$lower), hi = .s4(r$upper), trees = r$trees_used)
}
# isometry under the M3 adjustment set (E4)
rr_iso <- function(model) {
  r <- .rr_row(rr$E4, model = model, response = "isometry contrast lnM-3lnL")
  list(pct = .s1(r$pct_decade), lo = .s1(r$pct_decade_lo), hi = .s1(r$pct_decade_hi),
       z = .s(r$z), p = .rp(r$p))
}

rr_iso_therm_e1b <- rr_therm("E1b_detrended_anomaly", "isometry contrast lnM-3lnL",
                             term = "dT_detr", tbl = rr$E1)
rr_iso_therm_e2  <- rr_therm("E2a_locyear_random_intercept", "isometry contrast lnM-3lnL",

rr_iso_yr        <- rr_therm("E1a_anomaly_plus_year", "isometry contrast lnM-3lnL",

rr_n_shared <- local({
  e <- new.env(); load("../Analysis/data/derived/passer90.rda", envir = e)
  nrow(subset(e$passer90, !is.na(conc.wing.length) & !is.na(ln_body_mass)))
})
# temporal coverage within contributors for the wing sample (context for the
# within/between-contributor decomposition): contributors sampled over at least
# `span_min` calendar years, their records, and the share of capture-year variance
# lying within contributors
src_cov <- local({
  e <- new.env(); load("../Analysis/data/derived/passer90.rda", envir = e)
  d <- subset(e$passer90, !is.na(conc.wing.length))
  span <- tapply(d$Year, d$Main_researcher, function(y) max(y) - min(y) + 1)
  nrec <- tapply(d$Year, d$Main_researcher, length)
  yw <- d$Year - ave(d$Year, d$Main_researcher)
  span_min <- 10
  list(span_min = span_min, n_src = length(span), n_long = sum(span >= span_min),
       rec_long = sum(nrec[span >= span_min]),
       pct_within = sprintf("%.0f", 100 * var(yw) / var(d$Year)))
})
# the same temporal coverage within municipalities (context for the
# within/between-municipality decomposition, M5)
site_cov <- local({
  e <- new.env(); load("../Analysis/data/derived/passer90.rda", envir = e)
  d <- subset(e$passer90, !is.na(conc.wing.length))
  span <- tapply(d$Year, d$Municipality, function(y) max(y) - min(y) + 1)
  nrec <- tapply(d$Year, d$Municipality, length)
  yw <- d$Year - ave(d$Year, d$Municipality)
  list(n_site = length(span), n_long = sum(span >= src_cov$span_min),
       rec_long = sum(nrec[span >= src_cov$span_min]),
       pct_within = sprintf("%.0f", 100 * var(yw) / var(d$Year)))
})
# contributors and municipalities in the full sample and in the wing sample
prov <- local({
  e <- new.env(); load("../Analysis/data/derived/passer90.rda", envir = e)
  d <- e$passer90; w <- subset(d, !is.na(conc.wing.length))
  list(n_src = length(unique(d$Main_researcher)), n_site = length(unique(d$Municipality)),
       n_src_w = length(unique(w$Main_researcher)), n_site_w = length(unique(w$Municipality)))
})
# Methods counts pulled from passer90.rda (sampling hierarchy, provenance audit)
meth <- local({
  e <- new.env(); load("../Analysis/data/derived/passer90.rda", envir = e); d <- e$passer90
  w  <- subset(d, !is.na(conc.wing.length)); sh <- subset(w, !is.na(ln_body_mass)); m <- subset(d, !is.na(ln_body_mass))
  one <- function(x) { t <- tapply(x$Main_researcher, x$Municipality, function(s) length(unique(s)))
    list(single = sum(t == 1), n = length(t), pct = sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(t == 1))) }
  pc <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f", 100 * x)
  r2 <- function(f) summary(lm(Year ~ factor(f), data = w))$r.squared
  ea <- subset(w, Year <= 2006); la <- subset(w, Year >= 2013)
  s_ea <- unique(ea$Main_researcher); s_la <- unique(la$Main_researcher)
  list(n_shared = nrow(sh), one_sh = one(sh), one_m = one(m),
       site_multi = pc(mean(tapply(w$Main_researcher, w$Municipality, function(s) length(unique(s))) > 1)),
       src_multi = pc(mean(tapply(w$Municipality, w$Main_researcher, function(s) length(unique(s))) > 1)),
       r2_site = pc(r2(w$Municipality)), r2_src = pc(r2(w$Main_researcher)),
       lat_ea = sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", mean(ea$Latitude_decimal_degrees))),
       lat_la = sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", mean(la$Latitude_decimal_degrees))),
       alt_ea = .n(median(ea$Altitude, na.rm = TRUE)), alt_la = .n(median(la$Altitude, na.rm = TRUE)),
       src_ea = length(s_ea), src_la = length(s_la), src_both = length(intersect(s_ea, s_la)))
})
# REML checks quoted alongside the Stan estimates (glmmTMB, pooled over 50 trees)
cw_m5site_within <- .cw("M5", "yr_within_site")
cw_m6_unk <- .cw("M6")                     # unknown-sex wing records, full M3 controls
# residual-SD year effect with species intercepts in the residual-SD model (REML S6)
var_s6 <- local({ cm <- var_phylo$comparison
  r <- cm[!is.na(cm$tier) & cm$tier == "S6" & cm$component == "sigma" & cm$par == "scaled_yr", ]
  f <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%+.1f", x))
  list(b = f(r$pct_decade_phylo), lo = f(r$pct_decade_lo_phylo), hi = f(r$pct_decade_hi_phylo)) })
cw_ss <- cw_phylo$sample_sizes
n_anom_blocks <- nrow(cw_ss$anomalous_blocks); n_anom_rec <- cw_ss$anomalous_records
molt_unrec_pct <- sprintf("%.0f", 100 * cw_ss$molt_unrecorded_share)
# contributors that never recorded moult in the wing sample
molt_src_none <- local({
  e <- new.env(); load("../Analysis/data/derived/passer90.rda", envir = e)
  d <- subset(e$passer90, !is.na(conc.wing.length))
  sum(tapply(is.na(d$Molt), d$Main_researcher, all))
})
lrt_w$n_fail <- nrow(.lrt) - lrt_w$n
# the focal parameter with the largest per-tree R-hat, and the smallest per-tree ESS
rhat_top <- local({
  d <- bder$diag_terms; d <- d[d$variable != "sd_spp_int", ]
  top <- d[which.max(d$rhat), ]
  list(fit = top$fit, par = top$variable, n_gt_101 = sum(d$rhat > 1.01), n_terms = nrow(d),
       ess_bulk_min = .n(round(min(d$ess_bulk))), ess_tail_min = .n(round(min(d$ess_tail))))
})

# Introduction

Climate warming can alter animal morphology through several pathways: direct thermoregulatory selection, changes in resource availability, and developmental or evolutionary responses to a shifting environment [@gardner_declining_2011; @sheridan_shrinking_2011; @teplitsky_climate_2014]. These mechanisms have generated prominent predictions, most familiarly that endotherms should become smaller in warmer environments, because a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio aids metabolic heat dissipation [Bergmann's rule; @bergmann1847; @mayr1956; @ashton2002], and that heat-dissipating extremities such as bills should enlarge [Allen's rule; @allen1877; @ryding2021shape]. Both rules were formulated to describe spatial patterns, across latitudes and climates; the expectation that populations should shrink, or that their appendages should lengthen, as a given locality warms is a temporal extension of them and a separate hypothesis [@gardner_declining_2011; @teplitsky_climate_2014]. Empirical support for such general responses is, however, mixed. Broad syntheses indicate that morphological responses to contemporary warming vary substantially among traits, species, and ecological contexts rather than following a single directional pattern. @radchuk2019adaptive, synthesising phenotypic responses across wild populations, recovered no consistent systematic morphological response to warming. Understanding this heterogeneity requires determining whether the patterns documented in well-studied systems extend to ecological and geographic settings that are underrepresented in long-term datasets.

Multi-decadal morphological analyses have predominantly drawn on temperate, often migratory, bird species sampled through museum collections or long-term ringing stations in the Northern Hemisphere [e.g., @weeks2020]. Tropical communities, where avian diversity peaks, are far less represented, so it remains unclear how general the reported patterns are. Against this background, @jirinec2021morphological provides a valuable tropical investigation: analysing four decades (1979–2019) of standardised field measurements from 77 non-migratory understorey species in the continuous primary rainforest of the central Amazon (Biological Dynamics of Forest Fragments Project, BDFFP), they documented widespread declines in body mass alongside wing elongation in roughly a third of species, and interpreted the resulting reduction in wing loading as an adaptive shift towards flight economy in an increasingly warm understorey. Whether that pronounced Amazonian response is representative of tropical forest birds more broadly, or is instead strongly context-dependent, is the question we address here.

The Brazilian Atlantic Forest offers an informative contrast. It is a global biodiversity hotspot that differs from the continuous lowland central Amazon in almost every respect that might matter: it spans steep topographic and latitudinal gradients, and it has lost over 80% of its original forest cover, leaving the remainder divided among thousands of small, isolated fragments [@ribeiro2009atlantic]. It is therefore a useful test of whether the Amazonian pattern generalises to a tropical forest system with a very different landscape and thermal structure.

Two additional axes may help characterise whatever response is present. First, warming may act on phenotypic variance as well as on trait means, either widening among-individual variation through developmental instability or relaxed selection, or narrowing it through directional canalisation [@teplitsky_climate_2014; @debat2001mapping; @badyaev2005stress]. Second, morphological change may be driven indirectly through food supply rather than directly through thermoregulation [@schmidt_concomitant_2005; @teplitsky_bergmanns_2008]. If so, species that rely on different foods need not respond in the same way, and diet, from predominantly frugivorous or granivorous to strictly insectivorous, may help explain why some species change and others do not.

Testing this requires long series, and in most tropical regions these exist only as compilations of records from many research programmes. Trait databases such as ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS [@rodrigues_atlantic_2019] now assemble decades of field measurements across whole biomes, and mixed models can separate a temporal trend from the identity of the programme and site that supplied each record. This separation matters because programmes and sites rarely persist through a record. If those sampled late in a series differ from those sampled early, in measurement practice, protocol or habitat, a compilation can show a temporal trend that no population has undergone. How strongly such turnover can bias trends in compiled morphological data is seldom quantified.

Here, we use 24 years (1995–2018) of morphological data from 73 passerine species (`r .n(desc$n_rec)` live-capture records; ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS; @fig-map) to ask whether Atlantic Forest passerines show consistent morphological change across a period of regional warming. We characterise that response in three focal traits—body mass, wing length, and bill width—and then ask how it is structured: whether mass and wing length change in concert on the same individuals or depart from geometric isometry, whether morphology covaries with interannual temperature anomalies, whether residual phenotypic variability has changed, and whether diet explains variation among species. Because the data were compiled from dozens of research programmes whose sites shifted over time, we model contributor and municipality explicitly, test by simulation whether these models recover known trends in the real sampling structure, and compare the resulting rates with those of the central Amazon on a common scale.

# Results

## The region warmed while contributing programmes and sites changed

The analytical dataset comprised `r desc$n_spp` passerine species and `r .n(desc$n_rec)` adult live-capture records (`r .n(desc$n_rec_wing)` wing records across 72 species; *Herpsilochmus pectoralis* has no wing measurements in the compilation and enters only the analyses of the other traits), gathered between 1995 and 2018 at `r clim$n_localities` coordinate localities spanning the latitudinal and elevational range of the Brazilian Atlantic Forest, from sea level to over 1,500 m (@fig-map). Filtering criteria are given in the Methods.

![Geographic distribution and multi-decadal sampling of `r desc$n_spp` passerine bird species across the Brazilian Atlantic Forest domain. Sampling localities are displayed separately for the early (1995–2006; $n = 2,370$ wing records, 93 coordinate sites, 12 contributors) and late (2013–2018; $n = 2,870$ wing records, 146 coordinate sites, 33 contributors) sampling periods across the biome. Points represent sampling localities coloured by mean wing length, illustrating the broad latitudinal and elevational range covered by the dataset.](images/fig-map.png){#fig-map}

Historical climate data, available for `r clim$n_localities_with_data` of these localities (the remainder fall outside the WorldClim land mask; see Methods), documented regional warming over the study period: mean annual temperature rose by `r clim_t$b`°C/decade (95% CI: `r clim_t$lo` to `r clim_t$hi`°C/decade), representing an average warming of `r clim_t_tot`°C across capture sites between 1995 and 2018. In contrast, precipitation (`r clim_p$b` mm/decade, 95% CI: `r clim_p$lo` to `r clim_p$hi` mm) and drought indices (SPEI-12: `r clim_s$b`, 95% CI: `r clim_s$lo` to `r clim_s$hi`) showed no clear directional trend.

These records were contributed by `r prov$n_src` research programmes working in `r prov$n_site` municipalities (`r prov$n_src_w` and `r prov$n_site_w` in the wing sample), and both the set of active programmes and the geographic focus of sampling shifted substantially over the 24 years (@fig-map; Supplementary Fig. S1).

## Wing length declined weakly once sampling turnover was modelled, and responses varied among species

Model-free comparisons of per-species mean trait values between the early (1995–2006) and late (2013–2018) sampling periods, the lower and upper quartiles of capture year, showed substantial variation across species (@fig-trends): wing length decreased in 43 species and increased in 18 (@fig-trends A), body mass decreased in 36 and increased in 26 (@fig-trends B), and bill width decreased in 13 and increased in 31 (@fig-trends C).

![Species-level trajectories of wing length, body mass, and bill width between early and late sampling periods. Paired per-species means between the early (1995–2006) and late (2013–2018) periods for (A) wing length ($n = 61$ species), (B) body mass ($n = 62$ species), and (C) bill width ($n = 44$ species) across Atlantic Forest passerines. Lines connect period means for each species, coloured by direction of shift (red = decrease, blue = increase), illustrating the raw interspecific variation across the assemblage.](images/fig-trends.png){#fig-trends}

Unadjusted models suggested a relatively steep decline in wing length over time (baseline model: `r b_w0$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_w0$lo` to `r b_w0$hi`; `r b_w0_pct`%/decade; $P(\beta < 0) `r b_w0$P`$), but the estimated trend weakened substantially after accounting for contributor, municipality and the other sources of sampling turnover. In the fully adjusted model, the assemblage-level trajectory was modest and its credible interval overlapped zero: `r b_w3$b` mm/decade (95% CrI: `r b_w3$lo` to `r b_w3$hi`; `r b_w3_pct`%/decade; $P(\beta < 0) `r b_w3$P`$; @fig-wingtrend). The estimate was similar on complete cases (`r b_w3cc$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_w3cc$lo` to `r b_w3cc$hi`) and for log wing length (`r lw_m3$b`%/decade, 95% CI: `r lw_m3$lo` to `r lw_m3$hi`%; REML check), and slightly steeper, with an interval excluding zero, after removing `r n_anom_blocks` anomalous sampling blocks found by a post hoc screen (`r cw_noanom$dec` mm/decade, 95% CI: `r cw_noanom$dec_lo` to `r cw_noanom$dec_hi`; Methods; Supplementary Tables S1 and S5). Letting species slopes covary phylogenetically left the estimate similar but its interval much wider (`r b_w3pcor$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_w3pcor$lo` to `r b_w3pcor$hi`), and the phylogenetic share of slope variance was poorly constrained ($H^2 = `r h2s_w$b`$, 95% CrI: `r h2s_w$lo` to `r h2s_w$hi`), so the data do not tell us how far species' responses follow phylogeny.

Separating the year effect within and between contributors helped to locate some of the attenuation. Capture year varied substantially within contributors: `r src_cov$n_long` of the `r src_cov$n_src` contributors, holding `r .n(src_cov$rec_long)` wing records, sampled over `r src_cov$span_min` or more years, and `r src_cov$pct_within`% of the variance in capture year lay within contributors. The within-contributor slope was `r b_w5in$b` mm/decade (95% CrI: `r b_w5in$lo` to `r b_w5in$hi`; $P(\beta < 0) `r b_w5in$P`$); its interval includes both zero and the fully adjusted assemblage trend, so it cannot distinguish no change from a modest decline. Contributors whose records came, on average, from later years recorded shorter wings (`r b_w5btw$b` mm per decade of contributor mean year, 95% CrI: `r b_w5btw$lo` to `r b_w5btw$hi`; $P(\beta < 0) `r b_w5btw$P`$), a term estimated from only `r src_cov$n_src` contributor means. Municipalities offer less temporal replication: only `r site_cov$n_long` of `r site_cov$n_site` municipalities (`r .n(site_cov$rec_long)` wing records) were sampled over `r src_cov$span_min` or more years, and `r site_cov$pct_within`% of the variance in capture year lay within municipalities. The corresponding within-municipality slope (REML adjustment) was `r cw_m5site_within$dec` mm/decade (95% CI: `r cw_m5site_within$dec_lo` to `r cw_m5site_within$dec_hi`). The decompositions are therefore consistent with much of the steep unadjusted decline in wing length reflecting changes in sampling structure, but they do not establish how much temporal change remains within research programmes or sites.

To check that the adjusted model neither absorbs a real trend nor leaves an artefact in place, we planted known trends in `r rs_reps` simulated data sets per scenario that kept the real records, species, individuals, contributors, municipalities and years (Methods). With contributor and municipality effects independent of year, the fully adjusted model recovered a planted decline of −1.00 mm/decade almost exactly (mean estimate `r rs_clean_m3`). With contributor effects that drifted with contributors' mean capture year, calibrated to the gap between the real unadjusted and adjusted estimates, and no planted trend, the baseline model returned `r rs_art_m0` mm/decade and the fully adjusted model `r rs_art_m3`. Across scenarios, the 95% intervals of the fully adjusted model covered the planted value in `r rs_m3_cov`% of simulations. They excluded zero in `r rs_pow1`% of simulations with a planted decline of 1 mm/decade (about `r rs_mde_pct`% of wing length), in `r rs_pow05`% with 0.5 mm/decade, and in `r rs_fp`% with no trend (Supplementary Table S4). The data could therefore detect a wing decline of about 1 mm/decade with moderate power, but not one half that size.

Species-specific slopes from the fully adjusted model showed pronounced interspecific heterogeneity (@fig-species-slopes): `r sc$neg_point` of `r sc$n` species with wing measurements had negative posterior means, but `r sc$cri_spans_zero` of `r sc$n` had 95% credible intervals overlapping zero. Only `r sc$cri_neg` species declined with intervals excluding zero, and `r sc$cri_pos` increased. The median species slope was `r sc$median` mm/decade. Overall, wing-length trajectories were weakly negative at the assemblage level but highly heterogeneous among species, with substantial uncertainty around the average trend.

Hollow grey circles indicate baseline-model slopes.](images/fig-species-slopes.png){#fig-species-slopes}


## Body mass declined at about the Amazonian rate, but not consistently across species

Body mass showed no clear directional change across the 24-year record ($n = `r b_m3$n`$ records). The baseline estimate was modest (`r b_m0$b`%/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_m0$lo` to `r b_m0$hi`; $P(\beta < 0) `r b_m0$P`$). Under full adjustment it was `r b_m3$b`%/decade (95% CrI: `r b_m3$lo` to `r b_m3$hi`; $P(\beta < 0) `r b_m3$P`$), close in proportional terms to the fully adjusted wing-length trend (`r b_w3_pct`%/decade) but less precise, and within contributors it was `r b_mw$b`%/decade (95% CrI: `r b_mw$lo` to `r b_mw$hi`). Unlike wing length, the body-mass estimate changed little from the unadjusted to the fully adjusted model (Supplementary Table S2), and its interval still allows a decline of up to `r sub("^−", "", b_m3$lo)`% per decade.

On a common scale, this rate is close to the central Amazonian one. Across the 68 passerines of @jirinec2021morphological, mass changed by `r amz_m_dec`%/decade on average (species range `r amz_m_min` to `r amz_m_max`%; Methods), and per degree of local warming the two estimates are also similar (Atlantic Forest `r af_m_degc$b`% per °C, 95% CrI: `r af_m_degc$lo` to `r af_m_degc$hi`; central Amazon `r amz_m_degc`% per °C; @fig-amazon). What differs is consistency. In the Amazon all 77 species had lower mean mass by 2019, whereas in the Atlantic Forest 36 of 62 species decreased and 26 increased between the early and late periods (@fig-trends B). Wing length also differs: Amazonian wings lengthened by `r amz_w_dec`%/decade on average, whereas the fully adjusted Atlantic Forest estimate was `r af_w_pct$b`%/decade (95% CrI: `r af_w_pct$lo` to `r af_w_pct$hi`), with an upper bound that only just reaches the Amazonian mean.

Atlantic Forest: posterior means and 95% credible intervals of the unadjusted (open circles) and fully adjusted (filled circles) models, pooled over `r bz$n_trees` phylogenetic trees; wing length is converted from mm to % with the effect-scale factor (Methods). Central Amazon: mean change of the 68 passerine species in Table S6 of @jirinec2021morphological (diamonds), with the range of species means (bars). **(B)** The same fully adjusted rates per °C of local warming (Atlantic Forest: `r clim_t$b`°C/decade, without propagating its uncertainty; central Amazon: `r amz_warm`°C/decade, the bar spanning the wet- and dry-season warming rates reported by that study).](images/fig-amazon.png){#fig-amazon}


## Mass tended to be retained relative to wing length

We next asked how the two traits changed together, using `r .n(n_iso)` shared capture events in which wing length and body mass were measured on the same individual, across `r n_iso_spp` species. Under strict geometric isometry mass scales with the cube of wing length, so we modelled the isometry contrast $\Delta_{\text{iso}} = \ln M - 3 \ln L$ (Methods): it stays constant if birds shrink or grow without changing shape, increases if mass is retained relative to wing length, and decreases if birds become lighter for their wing length. We call this last pattern slenderisation, the direction of change reported for the central Amazon.

On these shared records, under full adjustment, wing length changed by `r b_lnw$b`%/decade (95% CrI: `r b_lnw$lo` to `r b_lnw$hi`%) and body mass by `r b_lnm$b`%/decade (95% CrI: `r b_lnm$lo` to `r b_lnm$hi`%; @fig-isometry A). Strict isometry would predict a mass change of `r b_iso_exp`%/decade from the wing trend alone. Fitted directly, the isometry contrast changed by `r b_isof$b`%/decade (95% CrI: `r b_isof$lo` to `r b_isof$hi`%; $P(\beta > 0) `r b_isof$Ppos`$), and by `r b_isop$b`%/decade (95% CrI: `r b_isop$lo` to `r b_isop$hi`%; $P(\beta > 0) `r b_isop$Ppos`$) under the parsimonious adjustment set. The direct estimate differs slightly from the contrast implied by the separate wing and mass fits (`r b_iso_sep`%/decade), because each model estimates its own species slopes and random-effect variances; the direct fit is the test of isometry. Both estimates point towards mass being retained relative to the wing, but in both the credible interval includes zero, so the shared-individual data do not exclude strict geometric isometry. Because body mass changed little, the contrast mostly reflects the uncertain wing decline. Phylogenetically covarying species slopes gave a similar estimate with a wider interval (`r b_isofpcor$b`%/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_isofpcor$lo` to `r b_isofpcor$hi`%).

In bivariate morphospace (@fig-isometry B), the assemblage estimate lies close to stasis and above the isometry line, not in the quadrant of longer wings and lower mass that corresponds to the direction of change reported for the central Amazon [@jirinec2021morphological], although the credible intervals of both traits include zero. Only `r n_iso_decoupled` of `r n_iso_spp` species had posterior mean slopes in that quadrant.

Points and horizontal bars indicate posterior means and 95% credible intervals, pooled over `r bz$n_trees` phylogenetic trees, for wing length, body mass, the mass change expected under cubic geometric scaling ($M \propto L^3$), and the isometry contrast ($\Delta_{\text{iso}} = \ln M - 3\ln L$, fitted directly under the full and the parsimonious adjustment sets). **(B)** Bivariate morphological state space ($\Delta\text{Wing}$ vs. $\Delta\text{Mass}$). The solid black line indicates strict geometric isometry ($y = 3x$), the dotted line indicates equal rates ($y = x$), and the shaded quadrant (longer wings, lower mass) marks the direction of change reported for the central Amazon [@jirinec2021morphological], which is shown as a direction only (@fig-amazon compares the rates). The green point is the Atlantic Forest assemblage estimate with the marginal 95% credible intervals of wing and mass change; the two traits were fitted in separate models, so no joint credible region is shown. Semi-transparent circles are species posterior means ($n = `r n_iso_spp`$).](images/fig-isometry.png){#fig-isometry}

## Annual temperature anomalies were not associated with the wing–mass relationship

If the wing–mass shift tracks thermal conditions, individuals sampled in warmer-than-usual years should be heavier or lighter for their wing length than birds caught in cooler years. We tested this with the local annual temperature anomaly at each capture ($\Delta T_{\text{local}}$; Methods).

We found no clear evidence for it. Under the fully adjusted set used for the temporal models, the isometry contrast was not associated with the annual anomaly ($\beta = `r b_thi$b`$ per °C, 95% CrI: `r b_thi$lo` to `r b_thi$hi`; $P(\beta > 0) `r b_thi$Ppos`$), and neither were wing length ($\beta = `r b_thw$b`$ mm per °C, 95% CrI: `r b_thw$lo` to `r b_thw$hi`) or log body mass ($\beta = `r b_thm$b`$ per °C, 95% CrI: `r b_thm$lo` to `r b_thm$hi`). The anomaly effect on the contrast was positive in every specification, but its interval always included zero, including with calendar year in the model ($\beta = `r b_thiy$b`$, 95% CrI: `r b_thiy$lo` to `r b_thiy$hi`), with a detrended anomaly, with a locality-year random intercept and with a baseline over every year from 1995 to 2018 (Methods; Supplementary Tables S3 and S6).

Anomalies of the year before capture, or of the two preceding years, were not associated with the contrast either (lag 1: $\beta = `r lg1_i$b`$, 95% CI: `r lg1_i$lo` to `r lg1_i$hi`; lags 1–2: $\beta = `r lg12_i$b`$, 95% CI: `r lg12_i$lo` to `r lg12_i$hi`; REML, 50 trees), nor with wing length or body mass. We therefore make no claim that interannual thermal variation drives any change in the wing–mass relationship.

## An apparent increase in bill width disappeared once contributors and municipalities were modelled

Raw species-level trajectories for bill width displayed both increases and decreases across species (@fig-trends C). In a baseline model without contributor controls, bill width appeared to increase (`r b_bl0$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_bl0$lo` to `r b_bl0$hi`; $P(\beta > 0) `r b_bl0$Ppos`$, $n = `r b_bl0$n`$), as Allen-type expectations would predict.

However, when contributor and municipality were accounted for, this apparent increase disappeared (`r b_bl1$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_bl1$lo` to `r b_bl1$hi`). In the fully adjusted model, bill width remained flat: `r b_bl3$b` mm/decade (95% CrI: `r b_bl3$lo` to `r b_bl3$hi`; $n = `r b_bl3$n`$). Temporal change within the same contributor was similarly flat (`r b_blw$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_blw$lo` to `r b_blw$hi`). The apparent baseline increase was therefore not robust to adjustment for contributor and spatial sampling structure, which were added together and whose contributions we cannot separate.

## An apparent rise in variability disappeared once contributors and municipalities were modelled

Heteroscedastic models estimated temporal change in the record-level residual standard deviation ($\sigma$) of wing length, that is, the variability remaining after the fixed and random effects of the mean model (Methods). In the baseline model, $\sigma$ appeared to increase by `r b_s1$b`%/decade (95% CrI: `r b_s1$lo` to `r b_s1$hi`%; $P(\gamma > 0) `r b_s1$Ppos`$). Adding contributor and municipality random intercepts to both the mean and the residual-SD models changed the sign of the estimate to `r b_s3$b`%/decade (95% CrI: `r b_s3$lo` to `r b_s3$hi`%), with the interval overlapping zero; with species intercepts also in the residual-SD model the estimate was positive again (`r var_s6$b`%/decade, 95% CI: `r var_s6$lo` to `r var_s6$hi`%; REML check). Adding local mean annual temperature to the residual-SD model yielded no association between residual variance and thermal conditions (`r b_s7t$b`% per SD of temperature, 95% CrI: `r b_s7t$lo` to `r b_s7t$hi`%).

Evidence for a change in residual variability in either direction therefore disappeared once contributor and municipality were accounted for, and residual variance was not clearly associated with local temperature.

## Diet did not clearly explain which species changed

To test whether diet attenuated or amplified wing-length trajectories, we used the share of invertebrates in each species' diet (EltonTraits), which runs from species feeding mostly on fruit and seeds to strict insectivores. In continuous interaction models (@fig-dietinteraction, top panel), the baseline model suggested a positive interaction between year and invertebrate share ($\beta = `r b_dA0$b`$ mm per SD of year per SD of diet, 95% CrI: `r b_dA0$lo` to `r b_dA0$hi`; $P(\beta > 0) `r b_dA0$Ppos`$). However, adding contributor and municipality intercepts halved this interaction to $\beta = `r b_dA1$b`$ (95% CrI: `r b_dA1$lo` to `r b_dA1$hi`; $P(\beta > 0) `r b_dA1$Ppos`$), with the credible interval spanning zero. Comparing invertebrate-dominated with other species (@fig-dietinteraction, bottom panel) gave a similarly uncertain interaction under the same controls ($\beta = `r b_dB1$b`$, 95% CrI: `r b_dB1$lo` to `r b_dB1$hi`).

The positive sign means that, if anything, species eating more fruit and seeds had steeper declines in wing length. Under the model with contributor and municipality intercepts, wing length changed by `r b_p10$b` mm/decade (95% CrI: `r b_p10$lo` to `r b_p10$hi`) at the 10th percentile of invertebrate share (`r b_p10$inv`% invertebrates), whereas the slope at the 90th percentile (`r b_p90$inv`%, strict insectivores) was centred near zero (`r b_p90$b` mm/decade, 95% CrI: `r b_p90$lo` to `r b_p90$hi`). Because the interaction itself is uncertain, diet did not clearly explain variation in wing-length trajectories, and we cannot exclude an effect of moderate size in either direction.
